attribution.note: Zitron's own 'In short' summary in his post. It builds on a Reuters Institute citation, but the sentence is his own assertion.

semantics.note: The proposition keeps both of his scopes: 'most' for company-led coverage and 'by default all' for mentions of OpenAI or ChatGPT. It is a present-tense observation about coverage.

contract.note: Using the period from ChatGPT's launch to the post, and reading 'most' as a majority and 'by default all' as effectively universal, are ordinary readings. Requiring a representative, generative-AI-specific coding of coverage is fair.

evidence.note: 2018 Reuters Institute study of UK AI coverage. It found about 60% of articles pegged to industry, but it predates the target period and covers AI broadly.

Found ChatGPT mentioned in 50–75% of post-launch AI articles at most outlets, with lower shares at a few. It counts ChatGPT only, not ChatGPT or OpenAI combined, covers broad AI news, and does not code who leads stories. It casts doubt on the 'all' part but does not settle it.

reviews.rationale: No evidence in the packet measures company-led share or combined OpenAI/ChatGPT mentions in generative-AI coverage for 2022–2025. e1 covers the wrong period and scope. e2 counts ChatGPT alone in broad AI news, so it falls short of the contract's contradiction standard. The evidence cannot settle either component.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his post.

semantics.note: A retrospective causal claim. He makes media coverage the dominant cause and free access the enabler. The proposition groups both under 'predominantly'; the contract correctly puts the predominance on media.

contract.note: It asks for credible causal attribution of adoption to media exposure, which is a fair test of 'predominantly the media's doing'. It correctly notes that publicity volume alone cannot show predominance.

evidence.note: OpenAI's launch post confirms ChatGPT was free at launch. This is a company disclosure and says nothing about media's causal share.

Danish worker experiment: information about ChatGPT had limited effect on actual adoption. The sample is narrow and the treatment is not sustained news exposure, so it cannot refute media predominance worldwide.

reviews.rationale: No evidence in the packet estimates how much of ChatGPT's adoption came from media coverage compared with usefulness, word of mouth, or workplace uptake. e3 only confirms free access. e4 is a narrow information experiment that does not address worldwide news-driven adoption. The causal claim cannot be settled.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his post.

semantics.note: Unhedged language ('accelerating at speed into a brick wall') predicting a collapse, with no deadline. 'Hype' is a fair gloss of executives incentivised to have companies valued on something other than what they sell.

contract.note: 'Brick wall' has no threshold. Reading it as a sharp, AI-linked tech collapse (a 20%+ index fall plus spillover or an investment cut) is ordinary and fair. Leaving the executives' causal role unscored is reasonable.

evidence.note: On 23 Oct 2026 the Nasdaq was about 5.8% below its 6 October high after an AI-spending sell-off. That falls well short of the 20% early-resolution threshold.

reviews.rationale: This is an open-horizon forecast with no deadline. The only evidence shows a sell-off of about 6%, which does not meet the early-resolution rule. The absence of a crash so far does not count as failure, so the forecast remains unscored.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his post.

semantics.note: The proposition keeps 'alone', the general scope (businesses in general), and both objects: sustainability/profitability and how people use the product.

contract.note: In context, 'tells you nothing' is hyperbole for 'does not establish'; his next sentences about daily versus occasional users confirm this. Testing the claim on the December 2024 300M announcement he was discussing is fair. A literal reading of 'nothing' would be too strong and would change the result.

evidence.note: Report reproducing OpenAI's 4 Dec 2024 announcement. The 300M figure is a bare weekly-active count. Message volume and paid-conversion rates had to be reported separately, which shows the count alone carries neither.
OpenAI company disclosure that some capabilities need much more compute, a cost factor the user count does not capture. Illustrative only.

reviews.rationale: Under the contract's plain reading, the December 2024 figure is an aggregate weekly-active count. On its own it does not show profitability, durability, how often people use the product, or what they use it for; separate figures were needed for those (e5). The result depends on reading 'nothing' as 'insufficient'. Read literally, the claim would be too strong.
